title: Second Regional Review Conference on Implementation of the Forest Rights Act Held in Kolkata
subtitle: Eight States reviewed progress on pending claims, record incorporation, Community Forest Resource Rights and PVTG Habitat Rights; district-wise, time-bound action plans called for
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 OCT 2026 12:31PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MoTA), Government of India, convened the Second Regional Review Conference on implementation of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) at Kolkata, West Bengal on 9th October 2026. The Conference brought together senior functionaries of the Tribal Welfare, Revenue and Forest Departments and Tribal Research Institutes of eight States, namely West Bengal, Assam, Tripura, Jharkhand, Odisha, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. Additionally senior officials of Andhra Pradesh were invited to share the best practices the State has undertaken on digitization, integration of FRA titles into government records and taking up proactive measures on convergence of livelihood schemes with FRA titleholders and providing credit facilities to the right holders. Further, District officials- Collectors, Sub Collectors and ITDP/ITDA Project Officers, where districts having a large pendency of FRA claims, also attended, to review the status of implementation and deliberate on a coordinated way forward. The Conference follows the First Regional Review Conference held in Bengaluru on 10 September 2026 for the Southern States.
Proceedings began with a Welcome Address by the Principal Secretary, Tribal Development Department, Government of West Bengal, who apprised the gathering of the objectives of the Conference and extended a formal welcome to the dignitaries and delegates which was followed by the Keynote Address of the Joint Secretary, MoTA, and the Special Address of the Secretary, MoTA.
In his Keynote Address, the Joint Secretary said that as on 31st August 2026, over 54 lakh claims had been received nationally, and about 25 lakh titles had been distributed. About 11 lakh claims still remain pending at different stages, while over 18 lakh claims have been rejected. He noted that Madhya Pradesh, Odisha and Assam account for substantial pendency concentrated in particular districts. He highlighted that the Regional Conference focuses on the following key priorities such as timely disposal of pending claims and review of rejected claims in accordance with the Act and Rules, reconciliation of FRA data, digitization of FRA case records, incorporation of recognised rights into revenue and forest records, accelerate recognition of Community Forest Resource Rights and Habitat Rights recognition for PVTGs.
In her Special Address, the Secretary, MoTA, said that the FRA places the rights, dignity and aspirations of forest-dwelling communities at the heart of inclusive and sustainable development. She appreciated the experience of Andhra Pradesh in digitization and creating of record of rights of FRA title holders to avail the post claim support, Odisha and Chhattisgarh in pioneering the recognition of PVTG habitat rights and recognition of highest number of IFR claims. She stressed that recognition of Community Forest Resource Rights (CFRR) must be matched by the capacity to exercise them. Gram Sabhas need support to prepare and implement Community Forest Resource Management Plans, and States should operationalise the joint advisory of MoTA and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. This advisory enables integration of these plans with the working and management plans of Forest Departments, while keeping the authority of the Gram Sabha central. She added that assistance is available under DA-JGUA for capacity building of Gram Sabha for preparation of such CFR management plans and their execution. She also called for PVTG-wise roadmaps for Habitat Rights which need to be prepared with sensitivity and the active participation of traditional institutions and the Gram Sabhas of all concerned villages. She further emphasised that recognised rights must be incorporated into Revenue and Forest records with accurate maps, and that convergence with programmes for productive land use, housing and livelihoods must become a regular part of implementation.
The Director, FRA, MoTA, presented the national scenario, including pendency in high-pendency States and priority districts. Her presentation also covered the importance of incorporating the Record of Forest Rights into revenue and forest records in line with the Ministry’s advisory of 24 June 2026 and Habitat Rights under the Ministry’s guidelines of 5 January 2026. She also outlined the financial support available from MoTA to take forward such interventions by the States. Further, states were also asked to reconcile data discrepancies and delays in Monthly Progress Reports. Also, States have been directed to prepare an action plan for strengthening Gram Sabhas to create awareness of FRA rights, post Claims support, and for preparation of the CFR management plan on priority. The Deputy Secretary, TRI & IT, MoTA, spoke on digitisation of FRA records and demonstrated the National-level FRA Portal and the FRA mobile app which can be useful to advance digitization, geospatial integration and decision-support systems for FRA governance. Also, urged the States to integrate their existing FRA records through Application Programming Interface (API).
State-wise Presentations
Officers of the eight States presented the status of FRA implementation in their respective States, covering claim pendency, incorporation of records, Community Forest Resource Rights and Habitat rights of PVTGs and digitisation of FRA records. The States also presented the action plan for timely disposal of pending claims, review of rejected claims, recognition of CFRR and habitat rights in a time bound manner and strengthening convergence so that eligible right-holders receive livelihood and development support.
The Conference concluded with a Valedictory Address by the Joint Secretary, MoTA, and a Vote of Thanks by the Director, FRA, MoTA.

title: MY Bharat–NSS Concludes First Month of Nasha Mukt Yuva Abhiyan with Nationwide ‘Yuva Sanwad Mela’; Engages Over 1.06 Lakh Participants

date:

content:
The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, through MY Bharat and the National Service Scheme (NSS), successfully organised the nationwide ‘Yuva Sanwad Mela’ on October 9, 2026, marking the conclusion of Month 1 of the 100-Week Sankalp Abhiyan under the theme ‘My Health, My Pride’. Conducted across 200 designated institutions and their adopted villages, the initiative recorded a consolidated outreach of 1,06,855 participants, bringing together young people and community members to strengthen awareness about substance abuse prevention and promote a healthier, addiction-free society.
Implemented across 15 NSS Regional Directorates, the Week 4 intervention achieved 100 per cent execution against the target of 200 institutions. The initiative engaged 93,662 youth participants and reached an additional 13,193 citizens through dedicated outreach activities in villages and slum communities. Moving beyond conventional pledge-taking activities, the Yuva Sanwad Mela emphasised interactive dialogue, public awareness and cultural expression to encourage informed conversations on the harmful effects of substance abuse.
The nationwide initiative featured three major components: youth dialogue, awareness stalls and cultural performances. Under the Youth Dialogue (Sanwad) component, 509 interactive seminars and open forums were organised, engaging 36,086 youth in discussions on the root causes of substance abuse, peer pressure and community-led prevention strategies, with participation from faculty members and local leaders.
Under the awareness component, NSS volunteers established 396 informational stalls and kiosks to disseminate information on the physical and psychological consequences of addiction and familiarise participants with available counselling resources. These activities engaged 32,909 participants. Complementing these efforts, 587 cultural performances, including street plays (Nukkad Nataks), skits and musical presentations, reached 24,944 individuals, using creative and locally relevant formats to communicate the message of an addiction-free India.
The campaign also demonstrated strong participation across genders. The reported youth participation figures recorded 48,269 female participants and 45,618 male participants, reflecting the active involvement of young women in the nationwide awareness drive. Through their participation, NSS volunteers and young people helped carry the message of health, well-being and collective responsibility into educational institutions and surrounding communities.
The grassroots mobilisation was further amplified through digital platforms, with young ambassadors generating 935 social media posts using the hashtag #NashaMuktYuva. These digital efforts extended the visibility of local activities and helped reinforce the campaign’s message among wider audiences.
The successful conclusion of Month 1 establishes a foundation for the next phase of the 100-Week Sankalp Abhiyan. Month 2 will focus on physical fitness and sports under the theme ‘Fit Youth, Addiction-Free Youth’, encouraging young people to adopt healthy lifestyles and recognise physical activity as an important component of substance abuse prevention.
Through the sustained participation of MY Bharat, NSS, educational institutions and local communities, the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports continues to strengthen youth-led awareness, community engagement and collective action towards the vision of a healthier, empowered and addiction-free India.

It also reinforces the message that the fight against substance abuse requires collective action, with families, communities, educational institutions and sporting icons playing an important role in guiding young people towards positive choices.
With Varanasi joining the 94th edition of Sundays on Cycle, the event will carry forward the spirit of collective fitness, youth participation and sporting excellence-bringing people together around one shared purpose: a healthier, fitter and drug-free India.
Fit India Sundays on Cycle is organised by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports (MYAS) in collaboration with the Cycling Federation of India (CFI), Raahgiri Foundation and MY Bharat. The cycling drive is conducted simultaneously across all States and Union Territories, including at SAI Regional Centres, National Centres of Excellence (NCOEs), SAI Training Centres (STCs), Khelo India State Centres of Excellence (KISCEs) and Khelo India Centres (KICs). Over 6,000 NAMO Fit India Clubs also organise the cycling initiative nationwide every week.

-

Lucha de Cholitas, Tinku, Rayuela, Trompo, Cachinas and Carrera de Sacos

title: Prime Minister Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana (PMDDKY)
subtitle: “One Year of Focused Agricultural Development Across 100 Districts”
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 OCT 2026 4:25PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Transforming Agriculture Through District-Level Action
India’s agriculture sector has significant potential across diverse regions and farming communities. However, despite rich potential, many areas face challenges like low productivity, inadequate irrigation, limited access to credit, and lack of post-harvest infrastructure. As a result, these areas are not able to attain their full agricultural potential and lag behind in economic development.
PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana (PMDDKY) seeks to address these gaps, and develop 100 Aspirational Agricultural Districts through focused intervention. By addressing district-specific needs the scheme can help unlock opportunities in productivity, irrigation, credit access, and post-harvest infrastructure.  PMDDKY was approved by the Union Cabinet on 16th July, 2025 for a period of six years, and was formally launched by Hon’ble Prime Minister on 11th October, 2025. It celebrates its first anniversary on 11th October this year.
The six-year initiative, beginning with 2025-26, focuses on transforming agriculture and allied activities across
100 Aspirational Agricultural Districts
. These districts were identified using three key indicators:
low productivity, low cropping intensity, and less agricultural credit disbursement
. The selection also considered the share of
net cropped area and operational holdings
in each State and Union Territory. Each State has at least one selected district.
The scheme is being implemented through the convergence of
36 Central schemes across 11 Ministries and Departments
,
State schemes and private sector participation
, enabling interventions suited to local agricultural priorities.
Administrative Structure for Implementation
The PMDDKY scheme follows a
three-tier implementation structure-
District Level:
The
District Dhan Dhaanya Krishi Yojana Samiti
, headed by the
District Collector/DM
, prepares and implements the
District Action Plan
.
State Level:
The
State Dhan Dhaanya Krishi Yojana Samiti
, headed by the
Chief Secretary of the State
, reviews and monitors the
District Plans
.
National Level:
Two committees oversee the scheme. The
National Executive Committee
is headed by the
Union
Minister for Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
. The
National Monitoring Committee
is headed by the
Secretary, DA&FW
.
District Action Plans
District Action Plans (DAPs)
are prepared based on the baseline and diagnostic analysis. The plans identify local agricultural needs and address them by converging relevant Central and State schemes. DAPs sets outcome-based targets, annual milestones, and interventions linked to relevant schemes.
DAPs are sent to the concerned State departments for incorporation into the respective annual action plans. This enables necessary approvals and fund release.
Progress is tracked through
121 indicators
across 36 schemes, comprising
74 output and 47 outcome indicators
. District performance on output indicators is ranked monthly through the PM-DDKY dashboard-
https://pmddky.niti.gov.in/
.
A Year of Implementation and Progress
The PMDDKY dashboard became operational in the
last week of October 2025.
Monthly output-indicator rankings began in November 2025, providing a mechanism for monitoring progress across the 100 districts.
All the 100 DDKY districts have prepared DAPs and it is under implementation.
Committees were constituted at the
State, District, and national levels
for review and monitoring.
All 100 districts submitted data against output indicators up to August 2026. All 100 districts also submitted outcome indicator data for the financial year 2025-26.
Central Nodal Officers are regularly reviewing the progress and guiding the districts.
Department of Public Enterprises has included adoption of DDKY districts for
CSR
activity by
CPSEs
for the
FY 2026-27 and 2027-28
.
The average score of the 100 districts across the six objectives increased from
18.85 in April 2026
to
46.89 in August 2026
, an improvement of
28.04 points.
Objective-wise average scores
also recorded improvement during the same period-
Enhancing Agricultural productivity:
1.50 to 8.08
Encouraging Crop diversification and sustainable agricultural practices:
4.08 to 10.18
Augmenting post-harvest storage capacity:
2.14 to 5.19
Improving irrigation infrastructure:
1.38 to 4.91
Enabling greater access to short-term and long-term agricultural credit:
2.40 to 6.53
Better governance & service delivery:
7.41 to 12.05
The first year also created platforms for farmers and Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) to exchange experiences and explore new opportunities. The
PM-DDKY FPO Sangam
, held in
December 2025
, brought together over
72 FPOs from 15 States and 33 PM-DDKY districts
. The event featured experiences on productivity, market access and income enhancement. It also covered natural farming, oilseeds, beekeeping, protected cultivation, micro irrigation, institutional finance and digital agriculture.
Best Practices from Dhan-Dhaanya districts
Local Processing, Better Price Realisation
In
Gadchiroli, Maharashtra
, a
PMDDKY district,
Desaiganj Farmers Producer Co. Ltd. (FPO), has
800 farmer members
. It has established a rice processing unit with
3 tonnes per hour capacity
and a
900 metric tonne (MT) warehouse
. The post-harvest infrastructure of its prized Jay Sri Ram rice variety enables local value addition and better price realisation. The FPO recorded a
turnover of Rs.1.24 crore in FY 2025-26
.
Better Markets, Better Returns
In
Tumakuru, Karnataka
, a
PMDDKY district,
Tiptur Farmer Producer Co. Ltd.
FPO
, has
750 farmer members
. It supplies ball copra to a French multinational company, enabling superior prices and market access for FPO farmers. The FPO recorded a
turnover of Rs.1.60 crore in FY 2025-26
and has aggregated
more than 138 tonnes of copra worth over Rs.1.9 crore as of 12 September 2026.
Smart Irrigation, Better Farm Productivity
In
Jaisalmer, Rajasthan
, a
PMDDKY district,
Jaisalmer Krishi Fed Producer Co. Ltd. has
1,236 farmer members
. The FPO practices Integrated Pest Management
(IPM)-based cumin cultivation across 2,000 acres.
It uses
solar-powered sprinkler irrigation across 500 acres
. The initiative promotes
efficient water use, renewable energy and improved farm productivity.
Building Agricultural Momentum Across Districts
PMDDKY completes its first year on
11 October 2026
, marking a year of focused district-level action. Across 100 districts, District Action Plans and indicator-based monitoring are now in place. District-specific interventions are supporting agricultural development on the ground. The progress achieved provides a foundation for stronger convergence and sustained agricultural development in the years ahead.

title: From Beacons to Landmarks:
subtitle: India’s Changing Lighthouse Story
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                10 OCT 2026 3:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
For generations, India's lighthouses were places people saw from a distance. Standing at the edge of the sea, they marked dangerous stretches of coast and guided vessels through darkness. Their lights belonged to sailors. Their towers belonged to the landscape.
With a coastline stretching over 11,000 km and
205 lighthouses
, India is now reimagining these historic maritime guardians. Today, the lighthouse is becoming much more than a distant landmark. Its first purpose remains unchanged: helping vessels navigate safely along India's coastline. Around that enduring role, however, a new chapter is taking shape. Lighthouse stations are being upgraded and opened to the public. Their maritime stories are finding space in museums, while their surroundings are being developed with pathways, gardens, amphitheatres and other facilities. Modern systems are strengthening the infrastructure that keeps their lights working reliably.
Lighthouse tourism has risen from about
4 lakh visitors in 2014 to 18.63 lakh in 2024–25
. Across the country,
75 lighthouses
have been developed as tourism destinations to preserve their historical and architectural significance. Some of these include the Mandvi Lighthouse and Dwarka Lighthouse in Gujarat, Tadri Lighthouse in Karnataka, Pamban Lighthouse in Tamil Nadu, and Vizhinjam Lighthouse in Kerala. A digital ticketing portal has also been launched under the Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships (DGLL), bringing the visitor experience onto a common digital platform. The growing interest in lighthouse tourism is creating new spaces to showcase India’s maritime legacy. These developments have also generated employment with nearby hotels, restaurants, tour operators, transport services, local shops, and artisans.
The Light Still Leads
The lighthouse may look much the same from a distance, but the technology behind its familiar beam has changed significantly. What once depended on fire and oil is now powered by the sun and strengthened by modern technology. All lighthouses in the country are solar-powered, making renewable energy part of the infrastructure that keeps these navigational lights working.
The evolution can be traced through individual stations. At Samiyani Island in Gujarat, an oil lamp gave way to a solar-powered electronic flasher, followed by an LED lantern in 2016. At Jodiya, a solar-operated flashing light was introduced before being upgraded to a high-intensity LED lantern in 2021. Lighthouses have become part of India's wider maritime information network.
87 Automatic Identification System
(AIS) shore stations have been installed on lighthouses along the coast. This ensures that the beam remains dependable, responsive and ready to guide vessels safely. AIS is a ship and shore-based data broadcast system in accordance with SOLAS (International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea). It is a powerful tool for enhancing situational awareness, thereby contributing to the safety of navigation and efficiency of shipping traffic management.
Lighthouse Museums: Bringing Maritime History Closer
While technology is strengthening the lighthouse's working role, its older stories are finding a place of their own. India has
dedicated lighthouse museums
at Chennai, Mahabalipuram, Alappuzha, Kannur, Muttom, Dwarka and Gopnath.
Mahabalipuram, also known as Mamallapuram, offers a particularly rich story, shaped by centuries of maritime activity along the Tamil Nadu coast. The Pallavas developed it as an important port during the seventh century AD for maritime trade with countries across Southeast Asia and the Mediterranean. A log fire once served as a guide for vessels approaching the coast. The first conventional lighthouse was established in 1887 on the roof of Olakkaneeswar Temple by placing a wick lamp inside a 4th-order optic and lantern. The Main light and emergency light source were modified to a cluster of three 150 W, 230 V metal halide lamps in 2004.
The present lighthouse is a 26-metre-high circular tower built with stone masonry. The tower itself has continued to evolve alongside the story it preserves. Its main light was upgraded to a
236-watt LED array in 2020
, the first of its kind. The result is a combination of living heritage and working technology.  The museum showcases a history of lighthouses through engaging exhibits and rare artifacts. Its National Heritage and Maritime Museum brings the site's past into the visitor experience.
This museum-led approach is also being carried into larger projects.
At
Lothal in Gujarat
, the National Maritime Heritage Complex (NMHC) is set to include a
77-metre-high Lighthouse Museum
. It is planned as the tallest lighthouse museum and one of the largest maritime museums in the world, with an estimated cost of
₹266.11 crore
. NMHC is one of the most significant cultural and maritime initiatives. It seeks to revive and showcase India's maritime legacy spanning over five millennia. It will also include a 5D Dome Theatre, Coastal States Pavilion, a Museotel, an Eco Resort and a Maritime Research Institute (MRI) being developed with the Indian Maritime University (IMU).  The lighthouse museum will captivate visitors with panoramic views of the entire complex. Its design draws inspiration from the Mahabalipuram Lighthouse, one of India’s oldest lighthouses. The museum will retain its distinctive architectural character, with extensive use of stone. Carefully curated virtual reality (VR) walkthroughs will offer visitors glimpses into the history of Indian lighthouses along the vast coastline. A state-of-the-art sound and light show will illuminate the lighthouse using projection mapping technology.
Lothal itself is one of the country's most important archaeological sites associated with ancient maritime trade. A lighthouse museum like this connects the earliest traditions of seafaring with the evolution of modern aids to navigation. The story is also expanding along India's eastern coast. A new
Lighthouse Museum at Visakhapatnam
is planned at the Old Lighthouse area, with
3,156 square metres of land
earmarked for the project.
When the Lighthouse Becomes a Celebration
The transformation has also created something that a conventional project rarely produces: a festival around the lighthouse itself. The first edition was held at Fort Aguada in Goa in 2023. The second moved to Puri in Odisha in 2024, while the third edition was held in Visakhapatnam in 2026. The festivals have deliberately placed lighthouses within a wider cultural setting. The first Indian Lighthouse Festival brought maritime heritage to life through cultural exhibitions, sessions on maritime history, classical performances, musical evenings featuring celebrity singers, and coastal cuisine.
The Indian Lighthouse Festival in Goa
The idea of community participation gained particular emphasis in the second edition of the festival. At Puri, the programme brought together lighthouse heritage with sand art, boat art, yoga, and folk dance & music. The event also highlighted Odisha’s five tourism-developed lighthouses, Gopalpur, Puri, Chandrabhaga, Paradip and False Point. The Government announced plans to involve coastal communities in preserving, protecting and promoting lighthouse sites.
During the Indian Lighthouse Festival 3.0 in Visakhapatnam, the lighthouse had become the centre of an even broader celebration of coastal identity. Local crafts, coastal cuisine and night-time illumination added colour to the programme, while families, youth, artists, entrepreneurs, students and visitors brought the festivities to life. Their enthusiastic participation made the celebration more vibrant, inclusive and closely connected to the communities around the lighthouse.
At Aguada in Goa, this new approach has taken a distinctly modern form. A
light-and-sound projection mapping show
has been introduced at the historic lighthouse, using the structure itself as a canvas to tell a new story around an old landmark.
Aguada Lighthouse
A New Course for the Lighthouse
The idea is no longer confined to India's coastal towers. It is now reaching new locations, while giving existing lighthouse sites a wider role in public life. An additional
25 lighthouses are proposed for development as tourism destinations
, expanding the network beyond the 75 sites already opened to visitors. Four lighthouses are being established along the Brahmaputra at
Pandu, Bogibeel, Silghat and Biswanath Ghat
. They will be India's first lighthouse infrastructure on an inland waterway with a combined outlay of about
₹84 crore
. Each lighthouse will rise to
20 metres
. Solar power and weather-observation sensors will add modern capabilities to the navigational infrastructure.
Yet these lighthouses are being designed for more than navigation. Each site will include a
museum, amphitheatre, cafeteria, children's play area, souvenir shop and landscaped public spaces
. The idea is simple but significant: a lighthouse no longer needs to be only something that marks a vessel's course from afar. It can also become a place that brings people closer to the water, its history and its changing possibilities. From coastal towers that have stood for generations to new lights rising along the Brahmaputra, India's lighthouse story is moving into uncharted waters. The light continues to serve its purpose, while the lighthouse becomes a destination in its own right.

title: PSA Prof. Sood Chairs Fourth All S&T Clusters’ Meet in Chandigarh, Calls for Stronger Collaboration and Technology Deployment
subtitle: संहतिः कार्यसाधिका - Fourth All S&T Clusters’ Meet Reaffirms the Power of Collaboration in Driving Innovation
ministry: Office of Principal Scientific Advisor to GoI
date:
Posted On:
                10 OCT 2026 8:46PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, Prof. Ajay Kumar Sood, chaired the Fourth All S&T Clusters’ Meet held on 9–10 October 2026 at Panjab University, Chandigarh, hosted by PU-IIT Ropar Regional Accelerator for Holistic Innovations Foundation (PI-RAHI). He was joined  by Dr (Mrs.) Parvinder Maini, Scientific Secretary and Dr Vishal Choudhary, Scientist-F, Office of the PSA. Prof. Meenakshi Goyal, Vice-Chancellor, Panjab University; Prof. Rajeev Ahuja, Director, IIT Ropar; Prof. Avinash Kumar Agarwal, Director, IIT Jodhpur; Prof. Rajat Sandhir, and Dr Pushpendra P. Singh, Director, PI-RAHI; and representatives of the eight S&T Clusters participated in the deliberations.
In his opening remarks, Prof. Sood noted that the Clusters have evolved into integrated ecosystems addressing regional, industrial, and societal challenges and increasingly functioning as “National Technology Accelerators.” He emphasised the need to strengthen inter-Cluster collaboration, stakeholder participation, coordination with RuTAG and RSVCs, and technology visibility. He also highlighted the growing global engagement of the Clusters, including the 12 international MoUs emerging from the First International Conference on S&T Clusters and subsequent partnerships with the University of Western Australia, India–Australia Smart Farm Network and UK Catapult Network.
During the inaugural session, Prof. Sood launched an Automatic Weather Station, highlighting the role of technology-enabled solutions in strengthening climate-smart and data-driven agriculture. The Meet also highlighted key inter-Cluster initiatives in sustainable mobility and clean technologies, including the inauguration of an EV Charging Station in Himachal Pradesh and the EVChargex Battery Swapping Station in Panchkula. The Himachal Pradesh initiative brings together charging infrastructure, EV users, and digital services, leveraging collaboration between DRIIV and PI-RAHI to support the State’s transition to electric mobility. The Panchkula facility demonstrates the transition of indigenous battery-swapping technology from pilot to commercial deployment, integrating EVs, batteries, rider onboarding, and digital management on a common platform. Prof. Sood also launched the report on Phycotree – Microalgal Photobioreactor, highlighting DRIIV’s efforts to facilitate the transition of indigenous technology from identification to field validation and potential deployment, including its engagement with GMR for applications at New Delhi IGI Airport; Kalaanubhav portal for PI-RAHI, featuring traditional crafts and products of artisans from Punjab and Jammu & Kashmir, along with an exhibition showcasing the work of artisans from Northern India; SPARKS 2.0; IGNITE 2.0; GINI 2.0; the STI Ecosystem of Northern India Reports; and an MoU signing ceremony. The Meet further marked the announcement of the UK Catapults–S&T Clusters collaboration in Healthcare, Emerging Technologies, and Net Zero Technologies, strengthening opportunities for technology development and international collaboration.
Scientific Secretary Dr Maini emphasised the need to build a connected National Cluster Network through sharing of technologies, infrastructure, expertise and industry partnerships. She highlighted inter-Cluster replication through D-PoC, Kalaanubhav and i-Passport, and called for stronger industry participation from R&D to validation, commercialisation, and scale. She urged the Clusters to focus on replication, collaboration and scale, translating successful regional solutions into larger national and global programmes.
A dedicated Stakeholders Meet on Strengthening S&T Clusters was also organised in Chandigarh, bringing together industry partners, CSR partners, academic institutions, and government representatives for interaction with the leadership of the S&T Clusters. The interaction provided an opportunity to discuss greater stakeholder participation and strengthen partnerships for technology development, validation, and deployment.
On the second day, Prof. Sood inaugurated a Digital Podiatric Clinic at the Panjab University Health Centre, Chandigarh, established by PI-RAHI under a CSR partnership from HL Klemove. The clinic is described as Northern India’s first Digital Podiatric Clinic and deploys AI-powered foot-screening technology for early detection and preventive care of diabetic foot conditions, bringing advanced medical technology closer to community healthcare. The delegates also visited the facility following its inauguration.
Prof. Sood also announced the 2nd International Conference on S&T Clusters, marking the next phase of the international outreach of the Cluster initiative. The announcement was followed by further deliberations on the present and future plans of the Clusters and discussions led by the Chair.
The two-day Meet provided a platform to review the progress of the eight S&T Clusters, assess their ongoing initiatives and discuss their present and future plans, with emphasis on technology translation, inter-cluster collaboration, industry engagement and strengthening regional innovation ecosystems. Cluster presentations and follow-up discussions were held across the two days covering the Pune Knowledge Cluster Foundation (PKCF), Jodhpur City Knowledge and Innovation Foundation (JCKIF), Bhubaneswar City Knowledge and Innovation Cluster (BCKIC), Delhi Research Implementation and Innovation (DRIIV), AMTZ-Vizag Cluster, Bengaluru Science and Technology Cluster (BeST), Research and Innovation Circle of Hyderabad (RICH), and PI-RAHI.
The Fourth All S&T Clusters’ Meet reaffirmed the importance of strengthening collaboration among the eight Clusters and building stronger linkages with industry, academia, government, and other stakeholders. The deliberations focused on taking forward Cluster-led initiatives, promoting technology deployment and creating greater opportunities for replication and scale-up of solutions across regions.
Conceived in 2020 following recommendations of the Prime Minister’s Science, Technology and Innovation Advisory Council (PM-STIAC), the Science and Technology (S&T) Clusters program of OPSA brings together academia, research institutions, industry, startups, government, and other stakeholders to address regional challenges through science, technology, and innovation. Over the years, the Clusters have evolved as regional innovation ecosystems focused on translating research and technology into solutions with societal and economic impact.
